extracted.intended_audience: journalists, newspaper editors, journalism students, and scholars of the press
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how newspapers and journalists should select, frame, verify, and present news—distinguishing the signaling function of news from the work of discovering truth, and recommending institutional and methodological supports for reporting complex social issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish news from truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The function of news is to signalize an event; the function of truth is to bring to light the hidden facts, to set them into relation with each other, and make a picture of reality on which men can act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only where social conditions take recognizable and measurable shape do news and truth coincide. Do not treat every news item as if it were the whole truth; recognize that much of reporting falls into the domain of argument and opinion rather than demonstrable fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge and verify source reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors are especially responsible for their judgment of the reliability of the source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not state as fact what rests on a source 'repeatedly shown to be unreliable.' Example: avoid writing 'Lenin Dead' when only an unreliable report exists; instead qualify attribution to the source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute unconfirmed claims precisely
rubrics_metrics.description: When information is unverified, present it as attributable — e.g., the news is not 'Lenin Dead' but 'Helsingfors Says Lenin is Dead.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear labeling of origins for doubtful reports so that the paper does not make the claim appear more certain than the source warrants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reducing complex causes to overt acts and stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: News is often uncovered by an overt act (demand, strike, disorder), and reporters/readers then invest these with familiar stereotypes rather than the complex underlying realities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive to report the deeper issues and context behind overt events (e.g., the working conditions leading to a strike) rather than treating only the event as the story; be aware that routine reporting and stereotypes disadvantage those whose grievances are complex and not easily signaled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance speed, economy, and accuracy in editorial judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors work under pressure of deadlines, fixed page sizes, competition, libel risk, and reader attention; this produces a preference for indisputable facts and routine judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize how these constraints shape selection and phrasing; where urgency pushes toward simplification, take extra care to avoid misrepresentation or undue compression of complex matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of propaganda and censored/secondhand reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: When access is closed (as with wartime or revolutions), reporting from centers of censorship and propaganda can create stereotypes and evoke hate and fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid uncritically adopting narratives from propagandistic or heavily censored sources; seek independent verification and resist sensational stereotype-based accounts of chaotic events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use standardization and routines, but be conscious of their distortions
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers depend on standardization, stereotypes, and routine judgments to produce a timely product and to economize time and effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ necessary production systems to meet deadlines while remaining vigilant that standard forms can flatten complexity and bias coverage; correct consciously and courageously where systemization misrepresents issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge uncertainty and the limits of journalistic knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists operate largely outside the realm of exact tests and should admit where there are no objective standards; much of what is reported beyond recorded facts is the reporter's version.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should make the uncertain character of the truth clear to readers, avoid presenting constructed versions as demonstrable truth, and disclose subjective limitations where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer objective, recorded facts where available
rubrics_metrics.description: News is precise in proportion to the precision with which the event is recorded; when an event can be named, measured, and made specific (e.g., public records), reporting can be factual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on documented records (court filings, official registers, quantitative data) for matters of fact; otherwise label material as argument or opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate organized intelligence and expert analysis for complex social reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex social issues require the assistance of experts, statisticians, auditors, and organized records; social scientists should prepare facts for decision rather than only explain decisions ex post facto.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop and use institutional sources, comparable records, and expert analyses to make social processes reportable and intelligible; press can prod social science and statesmen to produce usable formulations of social facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not expect the press to substitute for functioning institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: The press is too frail to carry the whole burden of popular sovereignty or to supply spontaneously the truth required for all public decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and communicate the limits of what journalism can reasonably accomplish; avoid adopting a standard of judgment that assumes newspapers must produce complete institutional knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of audience identification but avoid misleading framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Headline and placement decisions are matters of judgment about what will absorb a certain set of readers; news is often framed to provoke personal identification using stereotypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor presentation to readership without distorting importance or truth; avoid framing that manipulates reader identification to the detriment of accurate understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use imaginative empathy to enter into central issues
rubrics_metrics.description: To report beyond the obvious, the journalist should enter imaginatively into the lives involved so readers can step out of themselves and apprehend unfamiliar experiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Go beyond superficial catchwords and event descriptions; convey the human textures behind public incidents (e.g., foreman's temper, monotonous work, housing conditions) so readers can grasp the stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose and resist the tendency to sensationalize trivialities
rubrics_metrics.description: Without institutional records and expert sifting, news will tend to 'make of moles mountains, and of mountains moles' and focus on sensational aspects rather than substantive truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and reporters should resist yielding to sensational impulses driven by reader appetite for the curious trivial; cultivate standards that favor significance over mere excitement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize legal and commercial constraints on reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of editing and reporting is shaped by the law of libel, competition between newspapers, and the urgency of the buying public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for these constraints when making editorial choices but do not allow them to become excuses for systematic misrepresentation; balance risk and responsibility.
